content: 1. Sungsing T, Jantarapakde J, Pengnonyang S, et al. The Princess PrEP program in Thailand represents the first model where key populations themselves lead the delivery of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to other key populations. This innovative approach highlights the importance of community-led initiatives in addressing HIV prevention. (Sex Health. 2018;15(6):542–55). 2. Onovo A, Kalaiwo A, Emmanuel G, Keiser O. Community-led index case testing has emerged as a promising strategy to enhance HIV diagnosis and linkage to care among partners of key populations in Nigeria. This approach leverages community involvement to improve health outcomes. (Available at SSRN 3872626, accessed 24 June 2022). 3. Stardust Z, Kolstee J, Joksic S, et al. A harm-reduction approach to chemsex, led by the community, was implemented in Australia’s largest gay city. This case study underscores the importance of community-driven strategies in addressing substance use and sexual health. (Sex Health. 2018;15(2):179–81). 4. WHO. Consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis, and STI prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations emphasize human rights, gender equality, equity, inclusion, medical ethics, universal health coverage, and evidence-based public health. These principles guide interventions tailored to key populations. (Geneva: WHO; 2016). 5. Lillie TA, Persaud NE, DiCarlo MC, et al. An enhanced peer outreach approach was evaluated for its effectiveness in identifying new HIV cases among female sex workers and men who have sex with men in West and Central Africa. The findings demonstrate the value of peer-led interventions in HIV programs. (PLoS One. 2019;14(4):e0213743). 6. WHO. The framework on integrated, people-centered health services, presented at the 69th World Health Assembly, outlines strategies to improve health service delivery by focusing on the needs and preferences of individuals and communities. (Geneva: WHO; 2016). 7. WHO. Integrated care models provide an overview of approaches to deliver coordinated and comprehensive health services, emphasizing the importance of integration in improving health outcomes. (Copenhagen: WHO Europe; 2016). 8. International AIDS Society. Differentiated service delivery models aim to reduce the burden on health systems while improving access to HIV care and treatment. These models are tailored to meet the diverse needs of individuals. (Accessed 14 March 2022). 9. WHO. Youth-centered digital health interventions offer a framework for planning, developing, and implementing solutions in collaboration with young people. These interventions address the unique health needs of adolescents. (Geneva: WHO; 2020). 10. Hightow-Weidman L, Muessig K, Claude K, et al. Lessons from the Adolescent Trials Network for HIV interventions during COVID-19 highlight the potential of digital interventions to maximize youth engagement in health programs. (AIDS Behav. 2020;24(8):2239–43). 11. Ames HM, Glenton C, Lewin S, et al. A qualitative evidence synthesis explored clients’ perceptions and experiences of targeted digital communication via mobile devices for reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health. The findings emphasize the importance of accessibility and user-centered design. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019(10)). 12. Inhae C, Jiwon K. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examined the effects of mHealth interventions on sexual and reproductive health in emerging adulthood, demonstrating their potential to improve health outcomes. (Int J Nurs Stud. 2021;119:103949). 13. WHO. Technical briefs on HIV and young key populations, including those who sell sex, men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, and people who inject drugs, provide targeted guidance for addressing the unique challenges faced by these groups. (Geneva: WHO; 2015). 14. Bekker LG, Johnson L, Wallace M, Hosek S. Building the capacity of youth for the future is critical in addressing the HIV epidemic. This work emphasizes the importance of youth engagement and empowerment. (Wiley Online Library; 2015). 15. Patel P, Borkowf CB, Brooks JT, et al. A systematic review estimated per-act HIV transmission risk, providing valuable data for public health strategies and individual risk assessment. (AIDS. 2014;28(10):1509–19). 16. Kteily-Hawa R, Hawa AC, Gogolishvili D, et al. A scoping review examined the epidemiological HIV risk factors and underlying risk contexts for youth in the Middle East and North Africa region, highlighting the need for targeted interventions. (PLoS One. 2022;17(1):e0260935). 17. McLaughlin M, Amaya A, Klevens M, et al. A review of factors associated with the age of first injection among people who inject drugs provides insights into prevention strategies and early intervention opportunities. (J Psychoact Drugs. 2020;52(5):412–20). 18. Cornell M, Dovel K. Reaching key adolescent populations requires tailored approaches that address their unique needs and barriers to accessing HIV services. (Curr Opin HIV AIDS. 2018;13(3):274–80). 19. UNAIDS. A report on young people and HIV emphasizes the importance of addressing the specific vulnerabilities and needs of adolescents in the global HIV response. (Geneva: UNAIDS; 2021). 20. WHO. Guidelines for adolescent-friendly health services for adolescents living with HIV provide practical recommendations for translating theory into practice to improve service delivery. (Geneva: WHO; 2019). 21. WHO. Global standards for quality health-care services for adolescents outline a standards-driven approach to enhance the quality of care for young people. (Geneva: WHO; 2015). 22. WHO. A handbook for conducting adolescent health service barriers assessments focuses on identifying and addressing challenges faced by disadvantaged adolescents in accessing health services. (Geneva: WHO; 2019). 23. WHO. A global research agenda for adolescents living with HIV aims to generate evidence to support an AIDS-free generation. (Geneva: WHO; 2017). 24. WHO. Ethical considerations in planning and reviewing research studies on adolescent sexual and reproductive health emphasize the importance of protecting the rights and well-being of young participants. (Geneva: WHO; 2018). 25. WHO. Actions for improving clinical and prevention services for women and girls in high HIV incidence settings focus on integrating HIV prevention into contraceptive services. (Geneva: WHO; 2020). 26. Laurenzi CA, du Toit S, Ameyan W, et al. Psychosocial interventions for adolescents and young people living with HIV improve engagement in care and health outcomes, as demonstrated by a systematic review and meta-analysis. (Geneva: WHO; 2019).
